items.q: Anorexia nervosa diagnostic triad is what?
o: Restriction to low weight, intense fear of gain, body image disturbance
items.exp: DSM requires significantly low weight from restriction, fear of weight gain (or gain interfering behaviour) and image disturbance or failure to recognise seriousness. Others describe bulimia, binge eating and ARFID.
r: Incorrect. That is bulimia pattern.
Correct. Low weight, fear, image disturbance.
Incorrect. Binge disorder lacks compensation and low weight.
Incorrect. ARFID lacks image drive.
items.kp: Thin, terrified of fat, sees fat: anorexia.

items.q: Refeeding syndrome is driven by which electrolyte crash chiefly monitored?
items.exp: Insulin driven intracellular phosphate shift (plus potassium, magnesium) in depleted patients causes cardiac and respiratory failure days two to five; prophylactic replacement and slow calories prevent it.
r: Incorrect. Calcium not central mechanism.
Correct. Phosphate crash leads monitoring.
Incorrect. Sodium issues differ (water shifts).
Incorrect. Iron stores irrelevant here.

items.q: Which patients qualify high risk refeeding requiring lowest starting calories and daily bloods?
o: Very low BMI, little intake over 10 days, low baseline electrolytes or alcohol comorbidity
items.exp: NICE style criteria flag chronic depletion markers; bulimia at normal weight without depletion usually refeeds standardly. Protocols grade calories (often 5 to 10 kcal per kg start in highest risk) individually.
r: Incorrect. Near normal weight brief diet is low risk.
Correct. Depleted, low electrolytes, prolonged minimal intake.
Incorrect. Weight normal bulimia rarely high risk.
Incorrect. Single day fast depletes nothing.
items.kp: Starved long and low numbers: feed slowest.

items.q: First line psychotherapy for adolescents with anorexia nervosa is what?
o: Family based treatment (parents refeed, externalise illness)
No therapy until weight normal alone
items.exp: Family based (Maudsley) treatment empowers parents to renourish while separating illness from adolescent, outperforming individual therapy in youth. Adults receive CBT E, MANTRA or specialist supportive clinical management.
r: Incorrect. Individual alone weaker in adolescents.
Correct. Family based treatment leads youth care.
Incorrect. Analysis lacks eating disorder evidence.
Incorrect. Therapy accompanies restoration.
items.kp: Parents feed, illness blamed, teen absolved.

items.q: Bulimia nervosa physical signature set includes what?
o: Dental erosion, parotid enlargement, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, Russell sign
items.exp: Acid vomiting erodes teeth (perimolysis), swells parotids, wastes chloride and potassium causing alkalosis, and knuckles scar from teeth (Russell). Weight stays normal range unlike anorexia.
r: Incorrect. Those are starvation signs.
Correct. Vomit chemistry and trauma marks.
Incorrect. Weight normal or fluctuating.
Incorrect. Menses often preserved in bulimia.
items.kp: Teeth, parotids, potassium: vomiting leaves receipts.

items.q: Pharmacotherapy with best evidence in bulimia nervosa is what?
o: Fluoxetine (higher dose range) reducing binge purge cycles
items.exp: Fluoxetine around 60 mg patterns reduced bulimic episodes in trials as adjunct to CBT E; anorexia lacks effective drug for core weight restoration. Olanzapine shows only modest anorexia weight signal.
r: Incorrect. Olanzapine is anorexia adjunct research, not bulimia lead.
Correct. Fluoxetine adjunct in bulimia.
Incorrect. Lithium unrelated and toxic in purging dehydration.
Incorrect. Sedatives treat nothing here.
items.kp: Bulimia gets fluoxetine help; anorexia gets food.

items.q: Anorexia bone health best intervention is what?
o: Weight restoration and nutritional rehabilitation (plus calcium, vitamin D, DEXA monitoring)
items.exp: Energy restoration normalises hormones and bone accrual; hormone replacement without weight gain fails to restore bone, and adolescent bisphosphonates are specialist rare choices. Excess exercise worsens deficit.
r: Incorrect. Oestrogen without weight disappoints bone.
Correct. Restore weight to restore bone.
Incorrect. Not routine adolescent care.
Incorrect. Loading in deficit fractures risk.
items.kp: Feed bones back, pills alone cannot.

items.q: ARFID is distinguished from anorexia by absence of what?
o: Body image disturbance and fear of fatness
items.exp: Avoidant restrictive intake stems from sensory aversion, fear of choking or vomiting, or low interest, causing deficiency without shape weight drive. Treatment is exposure and nutritional rehabilitation adapted to cause.
r: Incorrect. Both can lose weight.
Correct. No body image drive in ARFID.
Incorrect. Deficiency occurs in both.
Incorrect. Avoidance defines ARFID itself.

items.q: Medical admission thresholds in anorexia prioritise which instability markers?
o: Bradycardia, postural hypotension, hypothermia, electrolyte disturbance, rapid loss
items.exp: Guidelines (MEED style) triage by physiology: resting bradycardia, postural drops, low temperature, syncope, electrolytes and trajectory, not BMI number alone, because deaths follow medical collapse.
r: Incorrect. BMI informs but physiology decides urgency.
Correct. Vitals and electrolytes instability.
Incorrect. Risk overrides preference conflicts via law when needed.
Incorrect. Duration chronicity differs from acuity.
items.kp: Slow pulse, cold and falling over: admit medically.

items.q: Binge eating disorder differs from bulimia by what and associates with what?
o: Binges with loss of control without regular compensation; obesity and metabolic risk
items.exp: BED lacks compensatory behaviours, driving weight gain and diabetes risk; CBT and structured programmes lead, with lisdexamfetamine licensed in some regions for moderate severe adults under specialist care.
r: Incorrect. Compensation absence defines separation.
Correct. No compensation, obesity association.
Incorrect. Adult onset common.
Incorrect. Weight often high.
items.kp: Binge without purge equals binge eating disorder.
